rendered: The document does not say that the EG process corroded the aluminium foil. It reports the opposite: the foil came out without corrosion. The paper says the EG-based process "fully recovered the aluminum foils with shiny surfaces," which suggests "that no corrosion occurred".[1][2] The authors also state that the process does not corrode the aluminium, citing XRD.[3] Corrosion of aluminium appears in the document only in a different context. Water was ruled out for delamination because the aluminium foil corroded in it, due to lithium leaching from the NMC cathode, which made the water solution basic. That corrosion would contaminate the NMC particles by forming Al(OH)3 precipitates on the cathode surfaces. More generally, the paper notes that aluminium foils are reactive and easily corroded during separation, which causes contamination of the active materials.[4][5][6][7][8][9][10] Because no corrosion occurred, there was no corrosion product to remove, and the document describes no removal step for any such product. The XRD pattern of the recovered foil shows peaks attributable only to aluminium, and EDX found no transition metals on it.[11][12][13][14] The only cleaning step the document describes is rinsing the delaminated cathode materials with alcohol to remove EG residues. It is not a step for removing corrosion products from the foil.[15][16]
